analysis.one_liner: Reauthorized and strengthened the Clean Water Act with toxic-discharge bans, sewer overflow cleanup, and fees on polluters.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Clean Water Act reauthorization bill with 6 Senate sponsors and three days of hearings in 1991 never got a committee or floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have renewed and expanded the nation's main water pollution law through 1998. It would have banned industrial discharges of highly toxic pollutants like mercury and PCBs, required over 1,000 communities to inventory and eliminate untreated sewage overflows, funded sewage treatment and state water programs, issued fish-consumption advisories, and protected workers who refuse to break pollution laws. It died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who swim, fish, or drink from public waters; residents of the more than 1,000 communities that discharge untreated sewage during storms; recreational and subsistence fishermen who would get state advisories on contaminated fish; wastewater plant workers; and tribal communities, whose treatment projects could be federally funded at 100 percent.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require EPA to publish regulations banning discharges of highly toxic, bioaccumulative pollutants — including mercury, PCBs, DDT, and dioxin (TCDD) — from industrial point sources.

States with combined storm and sanitary sewers would have to inventory overflows and submit programs and schedules to eliminate them; the bill's findings note that more than 1,000 communities discharge untreated sewage during storms.

EPA would publish biennial guidelines so states can issue advisories protecting recreational and subsistence fishermen from contaminated fish and shellfish, with technical assistance and public education.

The bill extends funding for state water pollution programs, state revolving loan funds, and combined-sewer-overflow grants, and allows grants covering up to 100 percent of sewage treatment project costs for Indian tribes.
It would be unlawful to fire or discriminate against any employee who refuses to perform duties that would violate the Clean Water Act or seriously injure the public.

States would have to require permit holders to pay annual fees covering at least 60 percent of the cost of administering point-source programs, giving regulators more resources than federal appropriations alone.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial dischargers face stricter effluent guidelines, discharge bans, pretreatment requirements, permit fees, and mandatory environmental audits. States must put up 50-cent matching funds for every federal grant dollar, and municipal treatment plants face operator certification, fees, and sewer overflow cleanup obligations whose costs flow to ratepayers and local taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial dischargers, states, and local utilities

drawbacks.text: The bill requires point-source permit holders to pay annual fees covering at least 60 percent of state program administration costs, a new cost for businesses and municipal utilities that can be passed to customers and ratepayers.
State grants would require non-federal matching funds equal to 50 percent of the federal allotment, a real cost for state budgets.
The bill would lengthen the required review cycle for effluent guidelines from five years to seven, slowing how often industrial limits are updated.
It would delete existing provisions on thermal discharges and heat standards, loosening one existing control in the law.
Fertilizer manufacturers would be barred from selling commercial fertilizer in the U.S. without water-quality precautions, raising their production costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong: the bill targets raw sewage overflows, toxic bioaccumulative pollutants, and contaminated fish — problems its own findings describe as widespread, including industries discharging roughly 360 million pounds of toxins directly to waters annually. The costs are real but mostly fall on the polluters and governments responsible: compliance spending by industrial dischargers, 50 percent state matches, and higher rates where local utilities must fix combined sewers. A few provisions modestly loosen the existing law — a longer seven-year review cycle for effluent guidelines and removal of thermal-discharge standards — but they are secondary to the bill's overall tightening.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got three hearings in the summer of 1991, and was never reported out of committee — so the full Senate never got to vote on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus introduced the bill on May 15, 1991, joined by five cosponsors — three Democrats and two Republicans, including Republican Sen. John Chafee, a senior member of the environment committee.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The subcommittee on environmental protection held hearings on June 13, July 9, and July 17, 1991, concluding them on July 18 with printed hearings S.Hrg. 102-325.
After the hearings, no further action was taken: the committee never voted to report the bill, and no floor vote ever occurred.
The bill expired with the end of the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial dischargers and fertilizer manufacturers avoided new discharge bans, stricter effluent guidelines, fees, and mandatory environmental audits. States avoided the new 50 percent matching requirement and the mandate that permit fees cover 60 percent of program costs, and no new federal clean water spending commitments were made.

for.name: Sen. Max Baucus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Water Pollution Prevention and Control Act of 1991 to amend and reauthorize the Federal Water Pollution Control Act.

for.name: Sen. John Chafee
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-RI), senior member of the Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan backing in the committee with jurisdiction.

for.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Subcommittee on Environmental Protection
for.what_they_did: Held three days of hearings on the bill in June and July 1991 and printed the record as S.Hrg. 102-325.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Quentin Burdick (D-ND)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee after the July 1991 hearings, keeping it from a Senate floor vote.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush's administration
against.what_they_did: The administration opposed the cost and scope of the 1991-92 Clean Water Act reauthorization effort, which contributed to the bill's failure to advance.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — three Democrats and two Republicans joined Sen. Baucus — and no vote record exists to show how the full chambers would have divided.

industries.industry: Industrial dischargers (chemical, pulp and paper, and other manufacturing polluters)
industries.note: The bill would impose stricter effluent guidelines, ban discharges of bioaccumulative toxins like mercury and PCBs, require pretreatment of toxic waste sent to public sewers, charge permit fees, and mandate environmental audits at noncompliant facilities. These are precisely the sources dumping an estimated 360 million pounds of toxic pollutants directly to waters each year, per the bill's own findings.
The bill prohibits manufacturing or distributing commercial fertilizer in the U.S. without precautions protecting water quality, a direct compliance cost for the industry.

Cities would face combined sewer overflow inventories, elimination programs, operator certification, and fees covering 60 percent of program costs, but the bill also authorizes federal grants, expanded revolving loan funds, and 100 percent federal funding for tribal treatment works to help pay for it.

Farms with runoff in impaired watersheds face conservation priority designations and possible easement acquisition, but nonpoint source grants and USDA soil conservation funding for priority watersheds would bring money into farm regions.

industries.industry: Environmental engineering, testing, and auditing services
industries.note: Mandatory environmental audits by certified auditors, operator training and certification programs, and a new technology demonstration grant program would create sustained demand for compliance testing, training, and pollution control services.
